title: Law Enforcement Access
subtitle: How authorised investigators find the provider behind any phone number, and request subscriber data lawfully, without a central database.
endNote: Read the specification and download the code at pstn2.org.

segments.text: Many believe the answer to phone fraud is a central database, holding one national copy of every number.
But here is the breakthrough insight. All of that numbering information already exists, in each provider’s own databases.
We don’t need to centralise it.
We just need to ask the provider that holds it.
Here is how a provider obtains all the available information about a phone number.
First, it checks its local cache, to see if it already has the answer.
Every PSTN2 response can carry an instruction to invalidate the cache, so cached values stay up to date.
If the cache has no entry, or the entry has been invalidated, the provider uses Ofcom’s S1 to S9 lists to find the Range Holder for the number block.
It then sends a request to that Range Holder.
The Range Holder may answer directly.
Or, if the number has been ported, it replies with a redirect, and the provider tries the new provider instead.
The provider updates its cache, and goes direct next time.
So there is no need for a central database.

scenes.title: Authorised parties use the same steps

segments.text: Any authorised party can find out about a phone number, using the same mechanism as a provider.
There is no need for cache logic, and existing manual processes can simply be followed.
Start with Ofcom’s S1 to S9 lists, to find the Range Holder for the number.
The Range Holder may answer directly, or send a redirect if the number has been ported.
Take a law enforcement officer who needs subscriber information for an investigation.
They open a simple JavaScript web page, either from the PSTN2 website, or as a local copy on their own machine.
The page queries the PSTN2 network directly: first the Range Holder, then the provider that now holds the number.
No central database to contact, and no single point of failure. Just direct queries to the providers.
The provider that holds the number already has the information an investigation may need.
Customer data: name, address, identity verification and account status.
Billing records and payment documents.
And calling history, including call detail records and message logs.
None of it travels through number discovery. It is released only in answer to a validated, lawful request.
A critical question: how does a provider know that a request is lawfully authorised?
Several options exist. Digital certificates, and requests routed through a Single Point of Contact.
Or time-limited access tokens, issued by a trusted identity provider.
A hybrid is recommended: digital certificates give cryptographic proof of identity, and OAuth tokens give fine-grained, time-limited access.
segments.say: A hybrid is recommended: digital certificates give cryptographic proof of identity, and oh-auth tokens give fine-grained, time-limited access.

segments.text: The authorities that will issue certificates and authorise requests still need to be identified.

scenes.title: One new field on Ofcom’s lists

segments.text: The root of all numbering information is each country’s regulator. This presentation focuses on the UK, and Ofcom.
The PSTN2 programme will also share how numbering data can be obtained in other countries, for global expansion.
For PSTN2 to work, the regulator adds one field to its numbering lists: the URL of the Range Holder for each number block.
Providers download and cache the lists, rather than querying them for every call. And other bodies can host copies, for resilience.
But the regulator may decline to host this field. Then another body would have to step in as the single source of truth.
That would create a new target for attack, and it would need strict governance.
So an early priority for PSTN2 is to persuade the regulator to host this one extra field on its numbering files.
And if a provider does not take part, and no Range Holder, wholesaler or MAP offers PSTN2 on its behalf, numbers in its ranges cannot be queried.
Visit pstn2.org to download working code, read the complete specification, and watch the other presentations in this series.

segments.text: They cover caller ID authentication, identification, encryption and direct routing, and electronic messaging to improve processes such as porting and 999.
All without a central database, or the costs that come with one. Just direct, verified queries to the providers, from any web browser.
